title: The Hymn of Harrow Glen
premise: Wendell Okonkwo returns to Harrow Glen to sell her late grandmother's house, only to find her childhood imaginary friend—Hollis—waiting on the porch, unchanged after twenty years. The tunnels she maps beneath the town hum with a song the residents have sung for generations, a hymn that keeps something in the old well asleep, and every singer eventually becomes part of it. Wendell, a lifelong skeptic, learns the song's first three verses from the town's dwindling faithful while refusing to believe any of it—until Hollis reveals that the last verse was never written down because it must be learned inside the well, and the well is refilling early. To survive, Wendell must descend, hold the melody in her mind without singing it aloud, and choose between saving the town by joining the choir forever or breaking the hymn entirely; she breaks it, silencing the well but erasing Hollis and every memory the town holds of her, ending the story as a stranger in her own hometown.
about_author: Coral Reyes is a former municipal surveyor who spent a decade mapping drainage systems across the American Midwest before turning to horror fiction. She writes in the margins of old plat maps and insists her best ideas come from tunnels that appear on no official record.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: Wendell arrives in Harrow Glen to inventory her grandmother's house, camera and laser mapper in hand. On the porch sits Hollis—exactly as she left him at nine years old, mud-stained overalls and all. She assumes grief-induced hallucination and photographs him anyway. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: uncanny unease wrapped in stubborn rationalism.

chapters.title: Plat Lines and Dead Ends
chapters.summary: Wendell surveys the property and finds a sinkhole behind the barn that no county survey acknowledges, breathing cool air in a slow rhythm. Hollis watches from the fence line, refusing to come closer. She logs the anomaly as a data point. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery shadowed by the sense of being observed back.

chapters.title: Everyone Sings Here
chapters.summary: At the general store, Wendell notices the clerk mouthing something while ringing her up—a melody, wordless, constant. An old man, Deacon Pruitt, warns her not to hum in the valley after dark. Hollis appears in the store's reflection, mouthing the same tune. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: creeping realization that the town shares a secret rhythm.

chapters.title: Hollis Speaks
chapters.summary: Night. Hollis finally talks, and his voice is exactly the voice she invented at nine: patient, slightly wrong. He tells her the well behind the barn is 'thirsty early this year' and that she was always meant to come back. Wendell records the conversation; the playback is static and a second voice beneath it. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: terror of the childhood comfort curdled into something else.

chapters.title: The Choir of Harrow Glen
chapters.summary: Wendell attends the town's Wednesday gathering in the whitewashed chapel, ostensibly for research. Forty residents sing a three-verse hymn; the melody matches the hum in her recordings. She notices the choir has no children, and the oldest singers' eyes are clouded like well water. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: outsider's dread hardening into investigative resolve.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: In the attic, Wendell finds her grandmother's journal—decades of entries about 'the debt,' 'the refill,' and a final page reading only: 'The fourth verse is not written. It is remembered. Do not remember it.' Hollis sits on the attic stairs, uninvited. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: grief transmuting into betrayal—her grandmother knew and never told her.

chapters.title: Descent, First Attempt
chapters.summary: Wendell ropes into the sinkhole with her survey gear. The tunnels are older than the town, carved with grooves that align like a musical staff. Her depth gauge reads impossible numbers. Halfway down, she hears her own voice singing from below and retreats. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: rational confidence cracking against physical wrongness.

chapters.title: Deacon Pruitt's Confession
chapters.summary: Pruitt, the last of the founding families' singers, tells her the hymn was a bargain: the town sings to keep the well's occupant dreaming, and the faithful who sing longest 'go down to hold the note.' His wife has been down there forty years. He begs Wendell to learn the hymn before the refill. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: reluctant empathy for people who chose complicity.

chapters.title: The Refilling
chapters.summary: Water rises in the old town well overnight, and the sinkhole's breath turns wet and warm. Livestock die facing the barn. The choir sings longer each night, and two singers collapse mid-verse, their mouths still moving. Hollis tells Wendell the refill is early because 'it heard you coming.' POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the dawning horror that her arrival accelerated everything.

chapters.title: Loyalty of Small Ghosts
chapters.summary: Wendell tries to leave; her truck dies at the county line three times, each time restarting only when she turns back. Hollis waits at the edge of town, and she realizes he's been guarding her—not trapping her. He admits he's the reason the thing below knows her name. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: anger at Hollis softening into terrible understanding.

chapters.title: Verse One, Learned
chapters.summary: Wendell begins learning the hymn—not to believe, she tells herself, but to understand. The first verse comes easily; it's a lullaby her grandmother sang. When she hums it alone, the tunnels answer in harmony, and every light in the house dies at once. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the seductive pull of belonging she swore to resist.

chapters.title: The Missing Year
chapters.summary: Wendell digs into town records and finds a gap: 1974, an entire year of missing minutes, a fire at the chapel, and her grandmother's name struck from the choir roster. A surviving photograph shows her grandmother mid-song with a second figure beside her—Hollis, unchanged. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the vertigo of discovering her own history was curated.

chapters.title: Pruitt Goes Down Singing
chapters.summary: Deacon Pruitt descends into the well voluntarily to 'hold the low note,' leaving Wendell his hymnal—blank pages except for instructions on breath control. The town's singing falters without him, and the water rises another foot. Wendell realizes she's now the only one who can learn the last verse in time. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the crushing weight of inherited duty.

chapters.title: What the Well Wants
chapters.summary: Hollis finally explains: the thing below doesn't eat people—it remembers them, perfectly, forever, and the hymn keeps it asleep so it can't remember the world awake. The last verse, sung, would wake it fully. Learned but never sung, it can seal the well for a century. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: clarity arriving too late to be comforting.

chapters.title: Verse Two, and the Cost
chapters.summary: Learning the second verse costs Wendell her reflection—mirrors show only the tunnel behind her. The town begins treating her as one of their own, setting her a place at tables, singing toward her house. She hasn't believed a word of it, and yet it's working on her anyway. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the erosion of the self she came here with.

chapters.title: The Night the Choir Broke
chapters.summary: The chapel congregation, down to nine voices, attempts the hymn without the low note and fails; the sound that comes up from the ground mimics their missing parts perfectly. Three more residents walk into the sinkhole at dawn, smiling. Wendell watches from her window, humming involuntarily. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: grief and guilt as the town pays for her hesitation.

chapters.title: Hollis's True Name
chapters.summary: Wendell confronts Hollis: he isn't her imaginary friend but the well's fragment—part of the dreaming thing that escaped and loved being a child's invention. He begs her not to descend, because if she seals the well, he goes back into the dark. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: love against duty, sharpened to a blade.

chapters.title: Verse Three, Sung Against Her Will
chapters.summary: The thing below, tired of waiting, sings through the town's sleeping residents—including, briefly, through Wendell. She wakes with the third verse in her mouth and blood on her lips from biting them. The well is one foot from the brim. She packs to leave and finds her truck already gone. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the last illusion of choice stripped away.

chapters.title: The Descent
chapters.summary: Wendell goes down with Pruitt's hymnal, a lantern, and Hollis walking beside her uninvited. The tunnels' grooves glow faintly with each verse she silently rehearses. At the bottom, the water is black and perfectly still, and something vast beneath it is listening to her heartbeat like a metronome. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: cold, focused courage—fear converted to purpose.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: At the water's edge, the well offers her the final verse freely—sung in her grandmother's voice, in Hollis's voice, in her own nine-year-old voice. To learn it she must listen without answering, hold every note in her mind while her whole body screams to sing along. She does, tears streaming, jaw locked. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: the hardest silence of her life.

chapters.title: The Sealing
chapters.summary: Wendell seals the well with the unsung verse, and the thing below begins to forget the world—forgetting the town, the hymn, and finally Hollis, who dissolves against her, whispering that being remembered by her was the only heaven he ever had. The water drains. The tunnels collapse gently behind her as she climbs. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: triumph braided with unbearable loss.

chapters.title: A Stranger in Harrow Glen
chapters.summary: Wendell walks out at dawn into a town that no longer knows her name, its chapel empty, its residents free and puzzled by their own sleepless years. The survey maps now show no sinkhole. She drives to the county line and the truck doesn't stop. In the rearview mirror, for one frame, a boy in muddy overalls waves. POV: Wendell. Emotional beat: bittersweet freedom—the price of survival is being forgotten, except by what sleeps below.
